sources_considered.why: Reports an Oxford Economics briefing on 2025 layoff data and AI attributions. It gives both the supporting judgment and the small-share counterpoint.
Quotes a Forrester report saying many firms announcing AI layoffs lack mature AI applications.
Quotes a Forrester analyst on CEOs who aren't deep into AI cutting staff. It also notes that some AI-linked cuts are plausible.
Covers a single company (Klarna). It is relevant background but not evidence of a broad pattern.

receipt.public_excerpt: Instead, it points to a more cynical corporate strategy: “We suspect some firms are trying to dress up layoffs as a good news story rather than bad news, such as past over-hiring.”

evidence_items.explanation: Oxford Economics looked at 2025 layoff data and concluded that some firms used AI as a positive gloss for cuts made for other reasons. This supports the idea that AI talk was used to justify layoffs.

evidence_items.publisher: PYMNTS (reporting Forrester via The New York Times)

receipt.public_excerpt: “Many companies announcing AI-related layoffs do not have mature, vetted AI applications ready to fill those roles, highlighting a trend of ‘AI-washing’ — attributing financially motivated cuts to future AI implementation,”

evidence_items.explanation: Forrester describes a common pattern: firms announced AI-related layoffs without AI ready to do the work, and attributed the cuts to future AI. This matches 'vague talk of AI to license their layoffs'.

evidence_items.locator: section 'Analysts play down scale of AI's current impact', paragraph 2

receipt.public_excerpt: “A lot of companies are making a big mistake because their CEO, who isn’t very deep into the weeds of AI, is saying, ‘Well, let’s go ahead and lay off 20 to 30% of our employees and we will backfill them with AI,’” he said.

evidence_items.explanation: An industry analyst says CEOs who don't understand AI well are making layoff mistakes. This echoes the second half of the claim. It is context only because the statement dates from after the target period.

evidence_items.publisher: Fortune (reporting Oxford Economics / Challenger, Gray & Christmas)

receipt.public_excerpt: While AI was cited as the reason for nearly 55,000 U.S. job cuts in the first 11 months of 2025—accounting for over 75% of all AI-related cuts reported since 2023—this figure represents a mere 4.5% of total reported job losses.

evidence_items.explanation: AI was cited in only about 4.5% of reported US job cuts in 2025. On a strict reading of 'often', this cuts against the claim that employers frequently invoke AI for layoffs.

unresolved_gaps: No source measures how many employers are vague about AI or misunderstand it. The evidence is analyst judgment ('we suspect', 'many companies').
Intent behind layoff announcements cannot be observed directly.
US-centric data; the claim is about employers in general.
